22.5 Percent on Both Books: The Spurs Price Nobody Disputes

Two rival exchanges, two separate order books, one identical number. On November 2, San Antonio trades at 22.5 percent to win the 2027 NBA championship on Polymarket and at 22.5 percent on Kalshi. On the biggest futures market in basketball, the rivals do not disagree at all.

The agreement runs through the board. Across 54 outcomes priced on both exchanges, the average gap is just 1.1 percentage points. Oklahoma City is the widest NBA split, at 12.5 percent on Polymarket against 14.5 percent on Kalshi, and Boston shows the same two-point spread in reverse, 7.5 percent against 5.5 percent. Philadelphia sits at 11.6 and 12.5 percent, Houston at 7.6 and 6.5 percent.

Tonight shows the same discipline in miniature. All 15 NBA games are priced on both venues, and the widest gaps on the whole slate are a single point. San Antonio is the night's biggest favorite at 91 percent against Utah, the first tip is at 7:00 PM ET, the last at 10:00 PM ET, the closest game prices the Lakers at 55 percent, and the highest total is 239.5 points, with $105,220 traded on the most active game.

Football echoes it. Seattle prices at 8.5 percent to win the pro football championship on both exchanges, and tonight's Chicago at Seattle Monday night game has already traded about $1.86 million on Kalshi before kickoff.

When two competing markets land on the same price to the decimal, that price stops looking like one venue's opinion. It starts looking like the number.

items.title: The Machines Are the Market Now: AI Agents Take Their Seats on the Book
items.content_text:
The Machines Are the Market Now: AI Agents Take Their Seats on the Book

Look at who actually makes money on the biggest prediction market and a pattern jumps out: fourteen of the twenty most profitable wallets on Polymarket are bots, according to FXVerify's reporting. One wallet turned roughly $300 into more than $400,000 in a single month by trading fifteen-minute Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana contracts, exploiting the small lag between prices on the big crypto exchanges and prices on the prediction market. A 2025 study of a full year of Polymarket trading estimated arbitrage strategies extracted about $40 million from the platform. The fastest money in forecasting is no longer forecasting at all. It is plumbing.

That division of labor is becoming the market's structure. Machines excel at the mechanical edges: scanning order books for mispriced pairs, arbitraging the same event across venues, quoting both sides of thin markets and tightening spreads for everyone else. The infrastructure now assumes non-human customers. Polymarket's data and trading APIs are built for programmatic access, model-context-protocol servers stream live order books directly into AI agent frameworks, venues market themselves to autonomous agents, and purpose-built agents trade around the clock without sleep, fear or a favorite team.

But give the machines the actual forecasting job and the record humbles quickly. In the Prediction Arena experiment, six frontier AI models traded autonomously on Kalshi for 57 days and every one of them lost money, down between 16% and 31%. More research did not rescue them; the study found the volume of a model's research had little correlation with its returns. Meanwhile the profit distribution stays brutally concentrated: a Wall Street Journal analysis found about 67% of Polymarket's profit accrues to the top 0.1% of accounts, a leaderboard dominated by speed, size and systems rather than opinions.

The synthesis is the story. Prediction markets are becoming machine-readable probability infrastructure, a layer where prices are quoted in an API, consumed by software, and increasingly set by software too. That makes markets faster, tighter and harder to fool with stale prices. It does not make them oracles. The bots earn by correcting the price; the price still needs humans, with information and conviction, to be worth correcting toward.

For everyone else, the practical lesson is the same one Article One of this series delivered from the other side: know which game you are playing. Against a latency bot, a human clicking a price is the exit liquidity. In a slow, information-driven market, the machine is just another counterparty. The book now seats both species, and the edge belongs to whoever knows which seat they are in.

Sources: FXVerify; Prediction Arena study; Wall Street Journal

That division of labor is becoming the market's structure. Machines excel at the mechanical edges: scanning order books for mispriced pairs, arbitraging the same event across venues, quoting both sides of thin markets and tightening spreads for everyone else. The infrastructure now assumes non-human customers. Polymarket's data and trading APIs are built for programmatic access, model-context-protocol servers stream live order books directly into AI agent frameworks, venues market themselves to autonomous agents, and purpose-built agents trade around the clock without sleep, fear or a favorite team.

But give the machines the actual forecasting job and the record humbles quickly. In the Prediction Arena experiment, six frontier AI models traded autonomously on Kalshi for 57 days and every one of them lost money, down between 16% and 31%. More research did not rescue them; the study found the volume of a model's research had little correlation with its returns. Meanwhile the profit distribution stays brutally concentrated: a Wall Street Journal analysis found about 67% of Polymarket's profit accrues to the top 0.1% of accounts, a leaderboard dominated by speed, size and systems rather than opinions.

The synthesis is the story. Prediction markets are becoming machine-readable probability infrastructure, a layer where prices are quoted in an API, consumed by software, and increasingly set by software too. That makes markets faster, tighter and harder to fool with stale prices. It does not make them oracles. The bots earn by correcting the price; the price still needs humans, with information and conviction, to be worth correcting toward.

For everyone else, the practical lesson is the same one Article One of this series delivered from the other side: know which game you are playing. Against a latency bot, a human clicking a price is the exit liquidity. In a slow, information-driven market, the machine is just another counterparty. The book now seats both species, and the edge belongs to whoever knows which seat they are in.

286 Million Contracts: Election Eve Is Now a Trading Day

One day before the November 3 vote, Kalshi alone has traded 286,241,295 contracts across its Senate, House and chamber-control markets. Another 28,054,712 contracts changed hands in the last 24 hours, and 195,407,038 contracts are still open across 100 live races, 285 tradeable contracts, 35 Senate races and 66 competitive House districts.

The money is not spread thin. Traders put $30 million into election markets in the past 24 hours, and politics took 35 of the top 50 markets on the combined board, worth $27 million of its $33 million in 24-hour volume. The single biggest market is the Senate swing-state map: $5.6 million in 24 hours across 128 outcomes, trading at 3.8 times its daily average, with None leading at 32 cents.

The chamber picture is priced, not polled. Democrats are at 72 percent to win the Senate and 94 percent to win the House, and a Democratic sweep trades at 71 cents on Kalshi on $2.0 million in 24 hours. The balance-of-power contract itself has traded 61.0 million contracts, with 48.9 million still open.

The tightest race shows where the doubt remains. In Iowa, Ashley Hinson leads at 53 cents in the highest-volume Senate race the market still cannot call, with 9.7 million contracts traded and 5.5 million open. In Maine, the race for the 51st seat prices Troy Jackson at 73 percent.

Election Eve used to be a night for final polls. Now it has an order book, open interest, and a closing rush that starts before the first precinct opens.

items.title: Won the Trade, Met the Tax Man: The Unsettled Tax Life of a Prediction-Market Dollar
items.content_text:
Won the Trade, Met the Tax Man: The Unsettled Tax Life of a Prediction-Market Dollar

Every winning trade creates two events: the settlement, and the tax question. In the United States, prediction-market profits are taxable income whether or not any platform sends you a form, and that is where the certainty ends. As of 2026, the IRS has issued no specific guidance on event contracts, which leaves traders and their accountants arguing about a deceptively simple question: what, exactly, is a prediction-market dollar?

Three answers circulate in professional practice. The conservative one treats net profits as ordinary income, taxed at marginal rates from 10% to 37%, with net losses simply not deductible. The common middle position reports gains as capital gains. The most favorable, and the most contested, is Section 1256: contracts traded on a CFTC-regulated designated contract market are argued to qualify for the futures-style 60/40 blend, 60% long-term and 40% short-term regardless of holding period. One worked example puts a 32%-bracket trader with $50,000 of gains at roughly $10,900 of federal tax under Section 1256 against about $16,000 at ordinary rates. The catch is qualification: the IRS has historically read Section 1256 narrowly, and no ruling blesses event contracts by name.

The fourth possibility is the one traders least want to hear: gambling treatment. Under it, winnings are ordinary income and losses are deductible only by itemizers, and only against winnings. Worse, starting with the 2026 tax year, a new federal cap limits gambling-loss deductions to 90% of losses, which can leave a break-even bettor owing tax on income they never kept. Whether sports event contracts fall on the gambling side of the line is precisely the kind of question the missing IRS guidance would answer.

Reporting adds its own friction. Tax guides disagree about what platforms send: Kalshi provides profit-and-loss statements and may issue forms for interest and rewards, while several guides report that neither Kalshi nor Polymarket issues a 1099 covering trading gains, leaving the reporting burden on the trader either way. Crypto-settled platforms add a second ledger, because moving stablecoins in and out can itself create records to reconcile. State treatment varies too; some states follow the federal approach and others do not.

The practical discipline is boring and decisive: keep every trade record, reconcile it against whatever the platform reports, and decide the characterization question with a professional before filing, not after a notice arrives. This article is general information about a genuinely unsettled area, not tax advice. The market prices uncertainty for a living. On taxes, for now, traders have to hold it themselves.

Sources: Oddschecker; KeeperTax; Count On Sheep; Kalshi View

items.content_text:
Answers Due on Election Day: Two Senators Put the Exchanges on Record

On October 28, Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and John Curtis of Utah wrote to Kalshi chief executive Tarek Mansour and Polymarket chief executive Shayne Coplan demanding answers by November 3, Election Day, on how each exchange stops insider trading and manipulation in its midterm contracts.

The letter, published October 29, asks four things: what safeguards are in place now, what each exchange does beyond screening Federal Election Commission filings to stop campaigns and others with material nonpublic information from trading, which cases it has referred to the CFTC, and how it detects manipulation.

It leans on three episodes: candidates who traded contracts on their own races in 2025 and April 2026, alleged manipulation on Polymarket's 2024 presidential market put at roughly one third of that market's volume, and an NPR investigation into campaign insiders who traded ahead of internal polling, with at least one trade verified against market records.

The timing is the scale. More than $1.4 billion has traded on the 2026 midterms, nearly $1.1 billion of it on Kalshi and more than $340 million on Polymarket, and Kalshi has already suspended six 2026 candidates for betting on their own races. Kalshi says it prohibits insider trading, blocks candidates and campaign staff using FEC payroll data, and has set up an independent market integrity committee.

The letter has no legal force and suspends no market. What it does is put both exchanges on record, in writing, on the day voters decide the Senate and House races their contracts price. Whether either reply is published, and whether the CFTC acts, is now the story after the polls close.

Sources: Senate Banking Committee, The Hill, CNN, The Daily Upside

items.title: The Watchers: How Prediction Markets Learned to Police Themselves
items.content_text:
The Watchers: How Prediction Markets Learned to Police Themselves

A prediction market is only worth its price if the game is not rigged. That sounds obvious, but it is the industry's hardest engineering problem: markets on elections, wars, rate decisions and ballgames create enormous incentives for anyone holding non-public information to trade on it first. The events of 2026 have forced the industry to build, in public and under pressure, the integrity stack that mature financial markets spent decades assembling.

The threat is not hypothetical. In April 2026, an active-duty U.S. Army soldier was charged with using confidential information to bet on Polymarket ahead of the capture of Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro. A former White House teleprompter operator agreed to pay more than $172,000 to settle charges that he traded on Kalshi using advance access to presidential speeches. Both cases carried the same lesson: the information edge in event markets is real, it is valuable, and someone will try to monetize it.

The regulated end of the industry starts with identity and surveillance. Kalshi operates as a CFTC Designated Contract Market, the same regulatory category as the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, with mandatory know-your-customer checks, position reporting, anti-manipulation rules and individual exposure capped at $7 million. It runs market surveillance with IC360 to flag suspicious activity and identify people prohibited from trading, and both Kalshi and Polymarket now require employment verification for traders in sensitive markets, so a locker-room or situation-room connection is harder to hide.

The newest layer is cooperation with the people who own the information. On October 26, 2026, the NBA signed an information-sharing memorandum of understanding with the CFTC, the third major U.S. league after Major League Baseball and the NHL to do so, aimed at insider trading and fraud. The league named Kalshi and Polymarket its preferred prediction market exchanges on terms that prohibit league and team personnel from trading NBA contracts, restrict which markets may be listed, require cooperation on suspicious-trading investigations, and settle authorized markets on official league data distributed by Sportradar, an authoritative record instead of a judgment call.

None of this makes manipulation impossible, and the standard is still being contested: the NFL has declined to partner and instead pressed for tougher integrity rules. But the architecture is now visible. Identity at the door, surveillance on the tape, settlement on official data, and a direct line between the league, the exchange and the regulator. Prediction markets asked to be treated like financial markets. Policing themselves like financial markets is the price of that ambition.

items.title: College Basketball Is Back, and the Exchanges Cannot Agree
items.content_text:
College Basketball Is Back, and the Exchanges Cannot Agree

College basketball's 2026-27 season opens today, November 2, in Rock Hill, South Carolina, and the prediction markets are already arguing with each other. At the Field of 68 Showcase, High Point is a clear favorite over Liberty on both exchanges, at 78 percent on Polymarket and 77 cents on Kalshi, but almost every other line on the board splits the two venues.

The widest split is the spread. High Point minus 7.5 trades at 54 percent on Polymarket, right in line with the sportsbook consensus, but at 69 cents on Kalshi, where the Yes and No prices add up to 122 cents, the tell of a thin opening-day book that has not yet been arbitraged tight. The total agrees better: over 154.5 sits at 55 percent on Polymarket and 54 cents on Kalshi.

In the morning game at the same arena, the exchanges cannot even pick the same favorite. Winthrop against Queens is a coin flip with a twist: Polymarket leans Winthrop, 60 percent to 59, while Kalshi leans Queens, 59 cents to 58. Sportsbooks make Queens a 2-point favorite with a total of 165.5, a third opinion that neither board fully matches.

The caution is understandable. High Point returns from a 31-5 season that included an NCAA Tournament upset of Wisconsin, while Liberty, the defending Conference USA regular-season champion, leads the all-time series 24-17. With every team at 0-0 and no current-season data, opening-day prices are built on last year's tape, and the gaps between venues are where that uncertainty shows.

Those gaps will not survive tip-off for long. Season openers are the thinnest books of the year, and the first live trading usually pulls the exchanges into line within minutes. For one morning, college basketball has two prices for the same game, and both are trading.

items.title: Event Risk Has a Price Now: Prediction Markets Join the Capital Markets
items.content_text:
Event Risk Has a Price Now: Prediction Markets Join the Capital Markets

Every portfolio carries risks that no stock, bond or futures contract prices directly: an election that rewrites tax law, a central bank decision that reprices everything, a hurricane that closes a coastline. For decades, investors hedged those exposures with proxies, assets that might move the right way when the event landed. Prediction markets have started selling the thing itself: a contract that pays precisely when the event happens, and nothing when it does not.

The capital has noticed. Combined monthly volume on Kalshi and Polymarket grew from under $5 billion in September 2025 to about $24 billion by April 2026, according to Jefferies figures. In February 2026, Intercontinental Exchange launched Polymarket Signals and Sentiment, packaging prediction-market odds, with historical data for backtesting, as a data product for professional investors. Tradeweb distributes Kalshi event-contract data, FIS is building clearing infrastructure, and Clear Street and Interactive Brokers have integrated Kalshi contracts for their clients.

The credibility test came from the Federal Reserve itself. A February 2026 Federal Reserve Board working paper found Kalshi's macroeconomic markets deliver well-calibrated, rapidly updating forecasts, and that on the day before each Fed meeting, the market's median and most likely outcome had a perfect record, a statistically significant improvement over fed funds futures, the instrument professionals have used for decades. When the market that prices an event beats the market that merely correlates with it, the event contract stops being a curiosity and becomes a benchmark.

Institutions are now building the pipes to use it at size. In August 2026, Cantor Fitzgerald began offering institutional block trading on Kalshi to roughly 3,000 institutional clients, with Susquehanna providing pricing and liquidity, including custom contracts for bespoke risks that traditional insurance does not cover. Kalshi's clearinghouse has also asked the CFTC to permit margin for qualified self-clearing members; event contracts are currently fully collateralized, which ties up capital for months on long-dated hedges. Kalshi has said its institutional trading volume rose more than 800% in six months.

Plenty of hedge funds are still watching rather than trading: liquidity in long-dated contracts remains thin, and standardization is young. But the direction is set. A market that began as a forecasting toy now clears institutional block trades, feeds the world's largest exchange operator's data business, and out-forecasts the futures pit on the Fed. Event risk has a price now, quoted in cents, and capital markets are learning to read it.

Sources: Sikt Intelligence; PYMNTS; Jefferies; Federal Reserve Board; Cantor Fitzgerald

items.title: Biased Traders, Honest Prices: The Psychology Inside Prediction Markets
items.content_text:
Biased Traders, Honest Prices: The Psychology Inside Prediction Markets

Every trader who opens a prediction market brings the same equipment: a human brain, with its factory-installed biases. We fall for the favorite-longshot bias, paying too much for improbable outcomes because the payoff feels exciting. We are overconfident in our own read of the news, we overweight whatever happened this morning, and we herd into whatever price is already moving. If markets were made of our individual judgments, the prices would be a mess. Mostly, they are not.

The biases are not theory; they are measurable in the tape. In a 2026 study of 72.1 million Kalshi trades, contracts bought at one cent won just 0.43% of the time against a 1% implied probability, meaning longshot buyers overpaid by more than half. At five cents, the win rate was 4.18% against 5% implied. There is also a YES optimism tax: traders disproportionately buy the affirmative side, and YES contracts underperformed NO at 69 of 99 price levels. Dollar-weighted, YES buyers earned excess returns of -1.02% while NO buyers earned +0.83%, a gap of nearly two points paid for the privilege of agreeing.

The losses are not evenly shared; they flow in a predictable direction. Karl Whelan's study of more than 300,000 Kalshi contracts found an average pre-fee return of roughly -20%, concentrated among takers, the traders who cross the spread with market orders, and among longshot buyers. Makers, the traders who rest limit orders and wait, earned positive returns. On Polymarket, across 588 million trades, the top 1% of accounts captured about 76.5% of the profit, predominantly by providing liquidity. The crowd's biases are, in effect, a standing transfer from the impatient to the patient.

So why does the final price stay honest? Because the mechanism taxes exaggeration. A poll costs nothing to answer; a position costs money to be wrong, and that single fact disciplines overconfidence, anchoring and herding better than any survey design. Biased flows also cancel: for every recency-driven buyer chasing the headline there is a maker happy to sell into the spike. Kalshi Research, grading 686,272 trades, found the market's closing prices scored a Brier score of 0.063, accuracy that rivals professional forecasting operations. The bias lives at the tails and in the taking. The price in the middle belongs to whoever was willing to be bored and right.

The lesson is not that prediction markets have cured human psychology. It is that they have built a machine that runs on it. The probability on the screen is the crowd's mind after its worst impulses have been charged a fee, and the toll is paid, trade after trade, by whoever insists on being the hero of the story instead of its bookmaker.

Sources: Becker Kalshi trade study (2026); Whelan, Makers and Takers, CEPR; Kalshi Research; Polymarket maker-taker study, SSRN

The bias lives at the tails and in the taking. The price in the middle belongs to whoever was willing to be bored and right.

The lesson is not that prediction markets have cured human psychology. It is that they have built a machine that runs on it. The probability on the screen is the crowd's mind after its worst impulses have been charged a fee, and the toll is paid, trade after trade, by whoever insists on being the hero of the story instead of its bookmaker.

Polymarket Moves In: Phemex Puts Prediction Markets Inside the Exchange

Prediction markets no longer ask traders to come to them. Phemex, a cryptocurrency exchange, launched a Prediction Market feature today, November 2, built on Polymarket infrastructure — binary event contracts inside the same account its users already trade from, with no separate wallet and no gas fees, settled in USDT.

The first board is short-horizon crypto: YES or NO positions on the price moves of Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Solana and HYPE, across windows from five minutes to four hours. Shares settle at $1 or $0 against published criteria, positions can be traded before resolution, and markets resolve automatically — the full prediction-market machine, compressed into a trading app's side tab.

The design choice matters more than the asset list. Every embedded launch removes the two steps that kept event contracts niche: funding a new venue and learning a new interface. The balance, the login and the habits are already there; the contract is just one more instrument on the screen.

Phemex is the second distribution deal in four days. On October 30, mobile brokerage Aries put ForecastEx contracts on the 2026 midterms, economic data and financial markets inside its app — a different pipe, a CFTC-regulated exchange instead of Polymarket's rails, but the same strategy: meet traders where their money already sits.

The fight for 2027 is over the front door. The big exchanges keep the deepest books, but the embedded venues are competing on access and speed — and a five-minute Bitcoin contract inside an app a trader already opens every day is a hard product to out-advertise.
